Question 12 — vulnerability management
OpenAI receives vulnerability reports through its security and safety bounty programs and provides an encrypted channel for reporting security incidents. Its disclosure policy also describes coordination for vulnerabilities found in third-party software and its role as a CVE Numbering Authority. 
For covered frontier systems, security assessments include red teaming, penetration testing and vulnerability scanning.
Question 13 — post-deployment practices
OpenAI disallows the use of our models and tools for certain activities and content, as outlined in our terms and usage policies. These policies are designed to prohibit the use of our models and tools in ways that cause individual or societal harm. We periodically update these policies in response to new risks and new information on how our models are being used. Access to and use of our models are also subject to OpenAI’s Terms of Use and our Business Terms. We employ a combination of guardrails, tools, policies, and processes to detect and enforce against abuse of our models. In addition to usage policies, we employ automated systems (for example, our Moderation API) and AI-powered tools to detect and prevent harmful content, human reviewers and expert investigators to conduct detailed investigations of model behavior and platform abuse, and external input to help our teams iterate on and regularly improve our moderation, detection, disruption, and enforcement capabilities. We publish information related to our post-deployment monitoring, mitigation and enforcement activities.
We build robust monitoring systems to detect potential model misalignment. We view model alignment as the primary lever to prevent potential misaligned behavior from our models. However, monitoring provides broad visibility into frontier model behavior, illuminating opportunities to further improve alignment and safety. This serves as an additional layer of protection against misaligned behavior that is detected.
Addressing vulnerabilities, incidents, emerging risks and misuse often requires participation from a number of teams across the company, including where applicable, teams responsible for research; safety and alignment; product; user or customer relationships and support; intelligence, investigations and teams supporting scaled detection and enforcement; security; policy teams; global affairs; legal and privacy; and communications.
Post-deployment, we rely on monitoring, user feedback, periodic security evaluations, and incident reporting to track risk emergence over time. Material findings can be fed back into model update cycles, safety classifiers, or policy adjustments.
Questions 14 and 14A — agentic systems and controls
Yes. Some of our products can perform supported tasks using tools and a cloud browser, including reading websites and completing multi-step workflows. It pauses when it needs user input, sign-in, or confirmation. Cloud browser documentation.
We design controls to help users remain in charge of an agent’s work. In our agentic products, users can manage website permissions, review consequential actions, and take over the cloud browser. OpenAI tests for prompt injection, phishing, and unintended actions, among other things.
We also train and test the agent to resist prompt injection: attempts to make it follow malicious instructions hidden in material it encounters, such as a webpage. Monitoring helps us detect and respond to these attacks. Secure browser takeover allows users to enter credentials without exposing those inputs to the model. Together, these measures address risks that arise when an agent uses outside information or works through services where the user is signed in.
Additionally, we train the model to be aligned with human intentions, and monitor for misalignment issues. This monitoring helps us detect and respond to issues as they arise in internal and external deployment, allowing us to iterate on further safeguard and evaluation development.

Excelya invests in research and practical initiatives that support responsible use of AI in regulated environments.
A major area of focus is Human-in-the-Loop (HITL), professional judgement, and human oversight in Medical Affairs, Medical Information, pharmacovigilance, regulatory, and compliance workflows. Our work examines what professionals need in order to exercise meaningful judgement when reviewing AI-assisted outputs, including access to evidence, decision authority, escalation pathways, and the ability to challenge or reject AI-generated content.
We are particularly interested in situations where individuals remain accountable for decisions supported by AI. Current work explores how organizations can prevent oversight from becoming a simple approval step and instead support genuine review, critical thinking, and professional responsibility.
Research topics include professional judgement, cognitive workload, automation bias, trust in AI systems, human-AI collaboration, auditability, and governance. The objective is to develop practical approaches that organizations can use to evaluate whether Human-in-the-Loop controls are effective in real-world regulated workflows.
We intend to share selected findings through scientific and professional channels. Planned outputs include a potential manuscript for Therapeutic Innovation & Regulatory Science (TIRS) and conference presentations or posters at events such as AISEAI. The goal is to contribute practical evidence and governance guidance for organizations that deploy AI in regulated environments.

Malt distinguishes between recommendation systems, generative AI and agentic AI. Generative systems receive additional controls for prompt and output security, factuality, privacy, provider processing and human review. Agentic systems, where applicable, require additional safeguards such as least-privilege access, approved tool lists, action limits, human confirmation for consequential actions and an effective interruption or shutdown mechanism. 
The lifecycle process is reviewed and updated under three circumstances: (1) when a new system version or model iteration is released, including consultation with the AI Deployment Committee for new algorithmic model baselines; (2) at least annually, including extensive independent penetration testing and a broader review of the effectiveness of governance, security, privacy, fairness and monitoring controls; (3) on an ad hoc basis, following an active model defect, vulnerability, operational exploit, material incident, significant performance or fairness degradation, major data or architecture change, new third-party dependency, regulatory development or material research finding.
For the plan and design stage, before developing or deploying an AI system, Malt defines in the design specifications its intended purpose, users, affected stakeholders, expected benefits, foreseeable misuse and potential risks. Systems are assessed in the risk mapping across privacy, security, fairness, transparency, accuracy, human rights, operational resilience and environmental considerations by the AI deployment committee. The review determines whether the system can proceed, requires additional safeguards or should not be deployed. 
In the collect and process data stage, Malt uses professional and marketplace information relevant to the service, such as skills and experience for matching and search. Malt evaluates data quality, completeness, and representativeness. Data is limited, cleaned, and tested, including for potential bias, before use. Users can correct, update, or request deletion of their information. Third-party models and AI services are subject to AI, privacy, security and contractual review. Data shared with external providers is governed by controls such as confidentiality, zero-retention policy, limited access. 
In the build, integrate, and interpret model stage, Malt’s matching systems use layered architectures combining lexical and semantic retrieval, ranking and business rules. Models, prompts, datasets, configurations and third-party dependencies are documented and versioned where relevant. Development and testing are separated from production environments, and access is controlled according to role and need. User-facing explanations focus on the purpose and limitations of AI-assisted search and recommendations rather than presenting the system as an autonomous decision-maker. Proposed candidates, and AI-generated briefs remain subject to human validation. Users can edit, reject or replace AI-generated recommendations and can use keyword search in the directory and type in manually their brief. 
Through the verify and validate stage, Malt verifies AI systems before and after material changes through a combination of automated testing, offline/online evaluation, human review, comparative experiments, security testing and fairness analysis. Malt also evaluates user group performance and potential disparities by including group analysis and counterfactual testing in which relevant characteristics are changed while professional skills and experience are held constant. These evaluations help identify differences in ranking position, visibility and exposure. 
Before release, at the deploy stage, Malt considers the evaluation results. Where appropriate, changes are introduced progressively and monitored against an approved baseline. Production systems maintain logging and traceability sufficient to investigate outputs, model versions, relevant inputs and human interventions, while respecting data-minimization requirements. Malt maintains human oversight for AI-assisted matching and recommendations. Fallback and rollback procedures are designed to allow Malt to isolate a faulty component, revert to a previously validated version or use a deterministic alternative when an AI component or external service is unavailable or behaving unexpectedly.
While in operation, Malt monitors AI systems across data quality, performance, fairness, security, reliability, user feedback and operational impact. Monitoring may include error rates, latency, anomalous behavior, user complaints, and external-provider failures. AI-related incidents may result in additional testing, changes to data or prompts, enhanced human review, rollback, temporary suspension, retraining or retirement of the affected system. Feedback from clients, freelancers, employees, researchers and other stakeholders contributes to continuous improvement.

Ubie does not use numeric capability thresholds, as we are not a foundation model developer. We apply decision criteria and governance processes instead.
Decision criteria. Severity is determined on two axes: imminence and severity of harm. Inputs are the use case, the users, the sensitivity of the data, the influence of outputs on clinical or health decisions, the degree of AI autonomy, whether human confirmation is in place, and whether an external foundation model is used. Because health and medical information can influence user behaviour, we treat three points as non-negotiable: our services provide general information; they do not constitute diagnosis or treatment; and they complement rather than replace human judgment.
How mitigations are graduated. Mitigations escalate with the assessed level of risk: (1) baseline - prompt and guardrail design, input and output filtering, disclaimers, terms of use; (2) elevated - mandatory medical review by physicians before release, sample evaluation of generative outputs, adversarial testing, and restriction of the intended purpose; (3) high - limitation of the scope of provision, access rights restricted so that highly confidential data is accessible only to the medical institution concerned, mandatory human confirmation with the original source always retrievable, and additional operational procedures and customer training; (4) unacceptable - postponement or non-release, or suspension of a feature already in service.
Generative AI and agentic AI. For generative AI features we assume that outputs of external foundation models may contain bias or hallucination, and we design for verification rather than trust: the original text is displayed by default with the AI-generated summary shown alongside (our "safety net structure"), sources are cited, and inputs and creation history are logged for ex post verification. Agentic AI systems that plan or act to a partial extent are under evaluation. Because an error in the medical domain can be irreversible, our governance for agentic capabilities requires an explicit boundary of autonomous action, a human decision point before any action affecting a patient or a medical record, transparency of the decision logic, and evaluation against the AISI Guide to Evaluation Perspectives on AI Safety in the Healthcare Sector before any phased introduction. Evaluation perspectives for agentic AI are being organised through our research organization Ubie Lab and the AISI Healthcare Sub-Working Group.
Governance. Risk assessment is performed by dedicated specialists independent of the development and business units in order to ensure objectivity. A two-layer structure - the Generative AI Promotion Team on the promotion side and the Risk and Compliance Committee (legal, security, public relations and other functions) on the risk side - shares information and deliberates trade-offs, and the Trust & Safety Team performs cross-product quality management. TELUS Digital employs a comprehensive and multi-layered approach to protect privacy and prevent unauthorized disclosure of confidential or sensitive data. Here's an overview of the key strategies and measures:
Data Classification and Handling:
Information is categorized into four main classifications: Restricted, Confidential, Proprietary, and Public.
All information assets are labeled based on sensitivity as 'Low', 'Medium', and 'High Risk'.
Appropriate handling schemes are adopted for each label and classification.
Access Control:
Implements the principle of least privilege, allowing only authorized access necessary to complete assigned tasks.
Access is restricted on a field-by-field basis, ensuring employees only have access to the data they need.
Utilizes role-based access control (RBAC) for critical assets.
Employs strong authentication mechanisms, including two-factor authentication.
Data Protection Measures:
Implements encryption or functionally equivalent technology for data protection during transmission and storage.
Prevents data exfiltration and mitigates the effects of exfiltrated data.
Employs malware defenses and email/web browser protections to minimize attack surfaces.
Network Security:
Utilizes firewalls, intrusion detection software, and other boundary defense mechanisms.
Manages and controls network ports, protocols, and services to minimize vulnerabilities.
Implements secure configurations for network devices such as firewalls, routers, and switches.
Monitoring and Auditing:
Collects, manages, and analyzes audit logs to detect, understand, and recover from potential attacks.
Actively manages the lifecycle of system and application accounts.
Conducts continuous vulnerability assessments and remediation.
Privacy by Design:
Embraces Privacy by Design principles, embedding privacy-enhancing measures into all processes.
Implements data minimization and ensures data quality.
Employee Training and Awareness:
Conducts security skills assessments and provides appropriate training.
Raises awareness about privacy obligations and data protection responsibilities.
Incident Response:
Maintains an incident response infrastructure with defined roles, training, and communication protocols.
Records and manages security incidents, including breach descriptions and recovery procedures.
Regular Testing and Evaluation:
Conducts regular penetration tests and simulates attacker actions to test defense strength.
Continuously evaluates the effectiveness of technical and organizational security measures.
Data Retention and Destruction:
Implements strict data retention policies aligned with legal and business requirements.
Ensures secure disposal of data, including physical destruction of media when necessary.
Third-Party Management:
Extends data protection requirements to vendors and third-party service providers.
Conducts due diligence on third parties who may have access to sensitive data.
Compliance with Regulations:
Adheres to various privacy regulations including PIPEDA, GDPR, HIPAA, and FCRA.
Maintains a Data Privacy Policy that is reviewed at least annually.
Physical Security:
Implements physical security measures such as access control, CCTV, and secure storage for hard copies of sensitive information.
Anonymization and Pseudonymization:
Applies these techniques to protect individual privacy when processing data for analytics or long-term forecasting.
Governance:
Appoints a Data Protection Officer to oversee data privacy compliance.
Maintains a robust data security governance program with senior management oversight.
Contractual Protections:
Uses confidentiality and non-disclosure agreements to legally bind individuals to protect sensitive information.
Penalties for Non-Compliance:
Enforces strict penalties, including termination and potential legal action, for unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information.

Specific risk identification practices for agentic AI capabilities, e.g., autonomous action-taking, tool use, multi-step planning (please specify): Microsoft has developed new threat modelling techniques for agentic AI and integrated them into its Security Development Lifecycle and Responsible AI Standard. These techniques reflect the distinctive risks created when AI systems combine models with tools, data sources, memory, and external environments to execute multi-step actions. They help teams map system architectures and trust boundaries, assess risks associated with tool permissions and agent actions, model potential misuse and failure scenarios, and design mitigations such as least-privilege access, human approval points, logging, and ongoing monitoring. To support implementation at scale, Microsoft has conducted internal deep-dive workshops involving more than 3,000 engineers, helping product teams apply these new threat-modeling techniques to agentic AI systems and integrate appropriate safeguards throughout the development lifecycle. The FGF's "advanced autonomy" capability thresholds directly address agentic risks by assessing autonomous task completion, tool use, and the ability to correct for complex error conditions [FGF p.13]. FGF capability elicitation explicitly tests models with multi-agent setups, prompt optimization, and tool/plugin connection to maximize performance on tracked high-risk capabilities [FGF p.6].
Assessment of risks arising from interactions among multiple AI agents
Multilingual and cross-cultural evaluation, including collaboration with local ecosystems (e.g., national AI institutes, language-specific evaluation consortia) for under-represented languages and cultural contexts (please specify): Microsoft is committed to advancing multilingual and context-relevant AI because language and cultural context are fundamental both to expanding access to AI’s benefits and to ensuring that AI systems are safe, secure, and reliable wherever they are deployed. As Microsoft highlighted at the India AI Impact Summit, language remains a significant barrier to AI diffusion, with AI systems often performing less consistently in digitally underrepresented languages than in English. Addressing this gap requires investment across the AI lifecycle - from locally relevant data and model capabilities to evaluation methods grounded in the languages, cultural norms, and real-world contexts in which AI is used. Expanding the geographic and linguistic coverage of AI research and evaluation can therefore help broaden the diffusion of beneficial AI while surfacing safety, security, and performance risks that English-first or translation-based testing may fail to capture. Microsoft is advancing these objectives through work on multilingual and multicultural evaluation, frontier safety and security, and community-centered AI research: • Microsoft is co-leading the MLCommons AILuminate benchmark’s multilingual, multicultural, and multimodal expansion in partnership with Google DeepMind, enabling more reliable measurement of AI safety and security beyond English and Western-dominant cultural contexts. The effort is currently focused on building the capability to assess performance of benchmarks in multilingual and multicultural contexts, working with partners to implement that capability in major Indic and Asian languages, with plans to develop an open source playbook that would accelerate expansion to other regions and additional APAC languages. • Microsoft contributed to the Frontier Model Forum's issue brief Emerging Practices for Multilingual Evaluations for CBRN and Advanced Cyber Risks (July 2026), which addresses the gap in safety and security evaluations for the highest-risk capabilities beyond English, and sets out best practices to build native evaluations across languages and cultures. • Microsoft is also advancing Samiksha, a community-centered method for evaluating AI behavior in real-world contexts, in collaboration with Karya and The Collective Intelligence Project in India. This work complements benchmark-based evaluation by helping incorporate the perspectives and lived experiences of the communities in which AI systems are used. • Microsoft signed a partnership with Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) in June 2026 to advance joint research and evaluation methodologies, including in multilingual AI safety. • Through Project Gecko, Microsoft is co-designing AI technologies with local communities in East Africa and South Asia to support agriculture, including the Paza family of automatic speech recognition models that can operate on mobile devices across six Kenyan languages, multilingual Copilots, and a Multimodal Critical Thinking (MMCT) Agent that can reason over community-generated video, voice, and text. We also launched PazaBench—the first automatic speech recognition leaderboard, with initial coverage of 39 African languages—and developed two playbooks for multilingual and multicultural capabilities, Paza and Vibhasha. This work also advances the New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments, which Microsoft signed alongside other leading AI developers and Indian innovators at the India AI Impact Summit in February 2026. The commitments reinforce the importance of strengthening multilingual and context-relevant AI evaluations and collaborating with local ecosystems to develop and apply evaluations for under-represented languages and cultural contexts.

The AI Deployment committee has decision authority when it comes to deploying AI models. 
The committee oversees the lifecycle of in-house AI developments and external AI tools being built into Malt's products across two key pillars: (1) new model/feature:  system risk classification, risks associated to the system, data protection and fundamental rights impact assessments, technical documentation check, transparency requirements check, and third-party vendor documentation (if applicable); (2) model/feature monitoring: review risks associated to the system, review incidents (if any), performance reviews and log retention audits (minimum 6-month retention). 
Before submission to the AI Deployment committee, the machine learning/product owner must compile a standardized AI System dossier containing the evaluation framework which includes notably a list of criteria, a description of what is evaluated and the assessment method, the design specification, data protection and fundamental right impact assessments, and a information security report from Malt’s information security team. 
The committee holds binding authority on system deployment under three possible outcomes: (1) approved: sign-off for deployment under specified operational parameters; (2) conditional approval: requires specific remedies (e.g., additional human-in-the-loop controls, refined dataset balancing) prior to go-live; (3) rejected / suspended: immediate block on deployment or mandate to halt an active model due to unmitigated high risk or serious incident reporting.
Safeguards include a mandatory progressive deployment scaling from 5% to 25%, 50%, and 100% user traffic, with reviews at each increment; real-time drift and error monitoring triggers an automated switch to a deterministic, rule-based fallback system.

TELUS Digital implements a comprehensive approach to secure testing throughout the development lifecycle. Here's an overview of when and how testing takes place in secure environments:
Separation of Environments:
TELUS Digital maintains separate development/test and production environments.
Access controls are in place to enforce the separation between these environments.
This separation ensures that testing activities do not impact the production environment and that production data is protected.
Testing Before Production Deployment:
All changes, including security patches and software configuration changes, are tested before being deployed into production.
This pre-deployment testing helps identify potential issues or vulnerabilities before they can affect the live environment.
Secure Testing Procedures:
Testing includes validation of various security aspects, such as:
Input validation to prevent cross-site scripting, injection flaws, and malicious file execution
Proper error handling
Secure cryptographic storage
Secure communications
Proper role-based access control (RBAC)
Data Protection in Testing:
Production data is not used for testing and development, or it is sanitized before use.
If confidential production data must be used in non-production environments, access is restricted to authorized personnel based on job responsibilities.
Test data and accounts are removed before production systems become active.
Continuous Vulnerability Assessment:
TELUS Digital employs continuous vulnerability assessment and remediation processes.
This ongoing testing allows for the identification and addressing of vulnerabilities throughout the system lifecycle.
Penetration Testing:
Penetration tests are conducted at appropriate intervals to ensure the integrity and confidentiality of systems.
These tests simulate real-world attack scenarios in a controlled environment.
System and Integration Testing:
Various types of testing are performed
Security Configuration Testing:
The initial configuration of systems or networks is documented, processed, tested, and approved in detail.
All subsequent changes to components are controlled through a robust configuration management process.
Patch Testing:
A documented patch management program is in place.
Patches are tested in a controlled environment before being applied to production systems.
Post-Implementation Testing:
After implementation, new systems are run in parallel with old systems to verify accuracy and reliability.
Post-implementation reviews are conducted to validate project completion and effectiveness.
Regular Security Evaluations:
Processes are in place for regularly testing, assessing, and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organizational security measures.
Separation of Duties:
Where possible, there is a separation of duties between personnel assigned to development/test environments and those assigned to the production environment.
This separation helps maintain the integrity of the testing process and reduces the risk of unauthorized changes to production systems.
Secure Testing of Third-Party Components:
For systems provided by third parties, TELUS Digital requires that these service providers undergo regular audits and provide attestation letters certifying compliance with security requirements.
Change Management in Testing:
All changes made to information systems are controlled to preserve confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
A configuration change control process is implemented at least yearly, ensuring that testing procedures remain up-to-date.

As our Frontier Governance Framework acknowledges, we also benefited from the advice of external experts in formulating our list of tracked high-risk capabilities for which we apply these governance steps. 
 
More broadly, external experts contribute to our evaluation practices in important ways. We identify third-party evaluators who have special expertise in evaluating specific risks, and we engage them to help us with tailored evaluations. These engagements help us better understand how to conceptualize certain risks and may surface opportunities for us to improve our risk mitigations.  
 
Specifically, external experts have contributed to our development of testing sets, including by writing and seeding prompts, and to our paradigms for red teaming and systematic measurement, with consultations with external subject matter experts helping refine our risk conceptualization. As highlighted in A Framework for Automated Measurement of Responsible AI Harms in Generative AI Applications, creating harm- or risk-specific measurement resources requires domain-specific expertise. They have also supported translation or localization guidance for AI evaluations. 
 
We also have in place mechanisms to receive reports from third parties of risks and potential vulnerabilities and incidents, including via reported via the Microsoft Security Response Center’s (MSRC) researcher portal, as described in Section 1E.

Microsoft's deployment decision-making process varies by the risk profile, consistent with Microsoft’s Responsible AI Standard, which was updated in 2026 to better reflect the roles Microsoft plays in developing or deploying the models, platform services, or applications with different risk profiles.
Decision authority. For frontier models subject to the Frontier Governance Framework (FGF), as described in our response to question 1A, the decision to deploy can only be made by Executive Officers or their delegates, based on a Recommendation for Secure and Trustworthy Deployment. For technologies or use scenarios triggering Sensitive Use criteria (including consequential impacts on legal status or life opportunities, risks of significant physical or psychological injury, or risks to human rights), the Sensitive Uses and Emerging Technologies team within the Office of Responsible AI works with relevant internal teams to assess risks, develop additional mitigations where needed, and determine whether Microsoft can proceed consistent with our principles and Responsible AI Standard. For other generative AI products, Microsoft implements risk-based launch-readiness reviews that may include centralized review processes or reviews by experts within our responsible AI governance community with product teams. From July 2025 to June 2026, we conducted pre-release reviews for nearly 2,500 generative AI features or products.
Evidence and criteria. Depending on a technology’s or use scenario’s risk profile, Microsoft may require pre-deployment evaluations across performance, safety, security, robustness, fairness, and privacy. For frontier models, a leading indicator assessment using state-of-the-art benchmarks screens for early indicators of tracked high-risk capabilities; triggering indicators then lead to a deeper assessment involving capability evaluation, capability elicitation, and holistic risk assessment, resulting in a risk classification of low, medium, high, or critical against capability thresholds.
Under Microsoft’s Frontier Governance Framework, models within scope undergo independent red teaming by Microsoft’s AI Red Team (AIRT). Where specified gating criteria are met, including based on the model’s assessed capabilities, risk profile, and relevant domain-specific risks, Microsoft also engages qualified and independent third-party evaluators to conduct additional testing.
Contextual caveats. Evaluation results should be treated as decision-relevant evidence. Microsoft’s own public research recognizes that AI evaluation remains an emerging science: results can be sensitive to how constructs, tasks, contexts and metrics are defined, and performance observed in controlled benchmarks may not generalize reliably. Microsoft therefore draws on multiple, complementary sources of evidence across the lifecycle, including pre-deployment benchmarks, capability and safeguard testing, red teaming and qualitative expert assessment, complemented after deployment by ongoing monitoring, incident and user feedback, and re-evaluation as systems, capabilities or deployment contexts change, as reflected in Microsoft’s 2026 Responsible AI Transparency Report.
Approvals and safeguards. As described in our response to question 1A, frontier model deployment requires tailored state-of-the-art safety and security mitigations applied before deployment and re-assessment post-mitigation. AI technologies and use scenarios that qualify for Sensitive Use reviews or generative AI release reviews may be required to implement various safeguards depending on risk profile, including staged release, content safety guardrails and prompt injection defenses, off-by-default settings, human review in agentic workflows, in-product disclosures, and broader transparency and feedback mechanisms [e.g., Smart Impression and Copilot Voice case studies].

How does your organization implement AI-specific information security practices pertaining to operational and cyber/physical security?
The security of our customer data and our products is our top priority, and we have specific measures in place that ensure robust operational, cyber, and physical security. 
For higher risk generative AI features and use cases, we have a robust review process that includes approvals from security, ethics, and product legal teams, among others.
When it comes to open-source models, we first run them on our own equipment or cloud accounts to ensure they comply with licensing guidelines.
For features that allow customers to use their own model, we provide secure storage for API keys and transparently disclose when customers are interacting with automated systems.
By default, we ensure human oversight is still required for high-risk or high-judgment decisions, and we apply strong security measures to protect system access. 
We also maintain distinct trust zones and ensure that access keys are not shared between production and non-production systems.
We have designed our incident response plans to address a wide range of risks, especially in the age of AI.
We build our products with a security-first mindset, including threat modeling that treats AI-generated content as crossing a trust boundary. 
We provide each Salesforce customer with the default security, out-of-the-box tools and educational resources necessary to protect their data. That’s why we have our Einstein Trust Layer with zero-data retention safeguards built into the platform. 
We also serve as a trusted advisor to our customers to help ensure they are also following security best practices and adopting proper controls, such as multi-factor authentication (MFA) and the principle of least privilege. 
How does your organization assess cybersecurity risks and implement policies to enhance the cybersecurity of advanced AI systems?
Our Security organization includes a Product Security Strategy & Advisory team, charged with ensuring that the existing and emerging risks that pose the greatest threats to our business and customers are taken into account throughout the company. The team performs in-depth discovery work aligned to the phases of the delivery lifecycle (secure design, development, and run) and red teaming to protect against key security risks like data exfiltration and prompt injection. We also maintain an insider threat program for our general operations.
The Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) recently revealed the top 10 LLM risks: prompt injections, insecure output handling, training data poisoning, model denial of service, supply chain vulnerabilities, sensitive information disclosure, insecure plugin design, excessive agency, overreliance, model theft. You can find a detailed account of how Salesforce is addressing the security risks here. 
How does your organization protect against security risks the most valuable IP and trade secrets, for example by limiting access to proprietary and unreleased model weights? What measures are in place to ensure the storage of and work with model weights, algorithms, servers, datasets, or other relevant elements are managed in an appropriately secure environment, with limited access controls in place? 
Access to Salesforce-hosted models is implemented in accordance with all other Salesforce production elements and conforms to existing security standards and best practices. The controls used include requiring Just In Time (JIT) credentials, Multi-factor Authentication (MFA), strong audit trails, and logging.
Requests to the models used by Einstein are required to pass through the Einstein Trust Layer, which implements strong authentication and authorization controls through OAuth. This ensures that only authenticated and authorized clients can access the model. We also use prompt defenses, rate-limiting, and watermarking to prevent theft of intellectual property and detect content for monitoring and alerting purposes.
Our AI, Data, and CRM products are hosted on Salesforce’s infrastructure platform, Hyperforce. Products running on Hyperforce benefit from its integration of enhanced standards for compliance, security, agility, and scalability, and from Salesforce's continued commitment to privacy.
What is your organization’s vulnerability management process? Does your organization take actions to address identified risks and vulnerabilities, including in collaboration with other stakeholders? 
Salesforce has a rigorous vulnerability management program to identify, assess, and remediate vulnerabilities across its products and services, assisting in the protection of customer data and data we hold as a controller. The program includes internal and third-party assessments, a bug bounty program, continuous monitoring, and engaging in threat intelligence information sharing programs to help surface and remediate known issues in third party hardware and software as early as possible in the vulnerability lifecycle. Salesforce uses a risk-based approach to prioritize and remediate identified vulnerabilities, following industry standards and best practices.  
How often are security measures reviewed? 
Security measures in our organization are reviewed at various intervals to ensure they remain effective and up-to-date. Information security policies, standards, and controls are reviewed annually. Our Information Security Management System (ISMS) Review Meetings are held semi-annually. Production Access (including access to our AI services) reviews are conducted quarterly, while privileged accounts are reviewed monthly. Separation of duties and privileges are reviewed every 30 days. Additionally, our security controls undergo continuous monitoring and are audited by external auditors for various security and compliance certifications at least annually.
Does your organization have an insider threat detection program? 
Salesforce has an insider threat program to monitor for potential risks posed by employees, contractors, or other insiders with privileged access to our systems. Salesforce also has a threat detection program designed to help our customers identify potential insider threats with access to their Salesforce data.
