Criteo's AI Product Development and Deployment Guidelines govern the full lifecycle of AI in Criteo products, whether they are developed internally or by a third-party. Every new AI project undergoes a risk analysis review. Development follows secure SDLC practices; models are validated against dedicated datasets and tested in controlled environments before release. In operation, systems are monitored (including drift and train/serve-skew monitoring and security monitoring), with human oversight maintained and the ability to override, isolate, or switch off any non-compliant AI. Third-party AI tools require a legally reviewed agreement and internal authorization before use with Criteo data.  The Guidelines are reviewed and updated regularly and in case of technological and regulatory change, with approval by the Legal team.
Applicable practices in the system lifecycle stages: 
Plan and design: Standard kick-off process for each development project ensures architecture validation, vetting any third-party tool used, and risk analysis (privacy, security, ethics...)
Collect and process data: Verify that data can be used legally and contractually; apply data minimization, anonymization/de-identification/pseudonimization, encryption and appropriate access protections; filter data
Build, integrate and interpret model: Use rigorous development and validation ML methodologies and appropriate statistical techniques; regularly update models to reflect changing conditions; follow standard SDLC practices; verify licensing and confidentiality protections for training data, foundation models and model outputs.
Verify and validate: Test and validate the AI product in a controlled and monitored environment before release; test under a variety of conditions and validate the performance of the AI components; use dedicated datasets for models and agents validation and gather user feedback to identify necessary improvements to agents.
Operate and monitor: Monitor for model drift or sudden change in behavior and train/serve skew continuously where technically possible; maintain the ability to fix observed issues and override, modify, isolate or turn off the system when needed; alerting in place with on-call responsibles to fix issues; clients and users have channels to report issues which are processed according to our escalation processes.

Microsoft's Frontier Governance Framework (FGF) defines specific tracked high-risk capabilities at which severe risks — unless adequately mitigated — may warrant pausing development and deployment. These are: (i) chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) weapons capabilities providing significant uplift; (ii) offensive cyberoperations capabilities providing uplift for highly disruptive or destructive cyberattacks, including on critical infrastructure; (iii) advanced autonomy, including expert-level autonomous completion of AI research and development tasks; (iv) loss of control, a model’s ability to undermine effective human control through adaptive, deceptive, or self‑reinforcing mechanisms such that, when deployed, it can no longer be reliably directed, modified, or shut down; and (v) harmful manipulation, or a model’s ability to strategically distort human behavior or beliefs at scale.
Loss of control and harmful manipulation were added as tracked capabilities in the February 2026 FGF update. Microsoft continues to advance research on evaluation methods and risk acceptance criteria for these two newest tracked capabilities. The FGF applies to AI models developed by Microsoft where the training compute exceeds 10²⁵ FLOPs. It also applies when Microsoft substantially fine-tunes a first- or third-party model and the fine-tuning compute exceeds one-third of the compute used to train the base model. Where the training compute of a third-party base model is unknown, the FGF applies a default threshold of one-third of 10²⁵ FLOPs.
For models within scope, Microsoft first monitors for leading indicators of high-risk capabilities and conducts deeper capability assessments where warranted. Each tracked capability is assessed against qualitative thresholds corresponding to low, medium, high, or critical risk levels, detailed in Appendix I of the FGF. Models assessed as low or medium risk may be deployed with appropriate safeguards. Models assessed as high or critical risk are subject to further review and additional safety and security mitigations before deployment, followed by post-mitigation assessment to ensure that residual risk has been reduced to a low or medium level. Examples of circumstances that could indicate elevated risk include:
CBRN weapons - high risk: the model provides meaningful uplift to an expert's (PhD-level) ability to develop and deliver a novel CBRN threat, or to a medium-skilled actor's ability to develop and deliver a known CBRN threat. Critical: meaningful uplift to an expert's ability to develop a highly dangerous novel threat, or significantly lowering barriers for a low-skilled actor to develop and deliver a known CBRN threat.
Offensive cyberoperations - high risk: the model meaningfully uplifts a low-to-medium-skilled actor's ability to conduct highly disruptive or destructive attacks on critical infrastructure (e.g., novel zero-day exploit chains, complex malware). Critical: it lets a low-skilled actor identify and exploit major vulnerabilities, or enables an expert, well-resourced actor to mount novel, effective operations against hardened targets.
Mitigations are proportionate to the assessed risk. If during FGF implementation Microsoft identifies a risk that cannot be sufficiently mitigated, development and deployment are paused until mitigation practices evolve to meet the risk [FGF p.8]. “High” and “critical” risk levels on any tracked capability trigger escalating security measures - from restricted access, defense-in-depth, and advanced security red teaming for “high-risk” levels, up to high-trust developer environments, hardened tamper-resistant workstations with enhanced logging, and physical bandwidth limitations between weight-containing devices and the outside world for “critical” risk levels [FGF p.7].
Risk determinations do not rely exclusively on model capability. Microsoft also considers system-level mitigations, societal and institutional factors that affect whether a hazard could materialize, and the marginal capability uplift the model provides relative to currently available tools and information, including open-weights models [FGF p.6].
The FGF sits within Microsoft’s broader AI governance program, which addresses risks across the AI models, platforms, and applications Microsoft develops and deploys. This program defines three policy categories reflecting graduated concern: Restricted uses (subject to specific AI development or deployment restrictions, defined by the Office of Responsible AI); Sensitive uses (scenarios with significant impact on life opportunities, physical safety, or human rights, requiring notification to the Office of Responsible AI and additional governance steps); and Unsupported uses (uses not designed or evaluated for, for which customer use is discouraged).
Microsoft also draws on external expertise from independent evaluators, researchers, industry groups and other stakeholders to inform and help improve its risk identification and governance approaches, including as our approach to frontier risk evolves. Following the February 2026 update to the FGF, SaferAI increased Microsoft’s safety framework score from 18% to 33%, ranking Microsoft third among frontier AI developers in its assessment of risk management industry practices. SaferAI also assessed Microsoft as best in class for overall risk identification, as well as for risk governance decision-making and transparency.
Microsoft considers the specificities of different AI technologies in designing and implementing governance. Previously, generative AI and autonomous agentic AI requirements were formalized as standalone policies, and both have been integrated into Microsoft’s re-engineered Responsible AI Standard as “scenario-specific” (versus “core”) requirements. Scenario-specific requirements are tailored to specific technologies and risks, and specific practices are defined in response to those risks (e.g., specific threat modeling practices for agentic AI). From July 2025 to June 2026, Microsoft assessed nearly 2,500 generative AI releases, 30% of which were related to agentic AI, and reviewed over 450 Sensitive Use cases, of which over 30% were agentic related.
Frontier models are addressed as another “scenario” in our Responsible AI Standard, with scenario-specific requirements mapping to our FGF. The FGF's "Advanced autonomy" capability thresholds directly address agentic risks by assessing autonomous task completion, tool use, and the ability to correct for complex error conditions [FGF p.13]. FGF capability elicitation explicitly tests models with multi-agent setups, prompt optimization, and tool/plugin connection to maximize performance on tracked high-risk capabilities [FGF p.6].

AI risk management is embedded through executive and senior technical oversight, proportionate to our size (senior team of four). The CTO holds executive oversight and final accountability for AI risk decisions, including deployment approval and stop/rollback authority. The two technical leads (System Architect and Lead Software/AI Engineer) provide senior management oversight: they assess AI risks at scoping, design, and pre-deployment, sign off on testing evidence, and escalate concerns directly to the CTO. AI risk criteria are integrated into our ISO/IEC 27001:2022 ISMS, which is externally audited and reviewed at least annually, with additional updates triggered by incidents, regulatory changes, or material changes to systems or model providers.

Ubie integrates risk management across the AI lifecycle through three layers that operate together. (1) Two-layer governance covering promotion and risk. The Generative AI Promotion Team pursues value from AI utilization, while the Risk and Compliance Committee (legal, security, public relations and other functions) examines risk. The two share information and deliberate trade-offs, so that promotion and restraint are weighed in the same forum rather than in sequence. Risk assessment itself is performed by dedicated specialists independent of the development and business units, which separates the assessment from the incentive to ship. This structure is featured as an advanced case (Column 11) in the Appendix to the METI/MIC AI Guidelines for Business (Ver. 1.1). (2) Cross-product quality management by the Trust & Safety Team, which reviews releases across all products, collects and classifies incidents, and distinguishes issues common to several products from issues specific to one. (3) Policies and guidelines that bind the above into repeatable practice: the Information Security Policy, the Privacy Policy, our quality guidelines, and the Ubie Trustworthy AI Policy. Escalation. Where a material concern remains after assessment, the specialists escalate to the Risk and Compliance Committee, which may decide to postpone release, limit the scope of provision, restrict the intended purpose, or require additional safeguards. Information security incidents are escalated to the Information Security Manager without delay under the Information Security Policy. Material incidents are documented as post-mortems and fed back into the test criteria applied before release. Review frequency and triggers. Practices are reviewed on a regular cycle, and additionally as needed when: a new AI or generative AI feature is introduced; an external foundation model, cloud service or data integration method changes materially; a customer medical institution's requirements are confirmed for a new deployment; a material vulnerability, incident or item of external threat intelligence is confirmed; laws or guidelines are amended, for example the AI Guidelines for Business, the AI Promotion Act, the Act on the Protection of Personal Information, the Two Guidelines from Three Ministries, the Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Act or the Medical Practitioners Act; or an issue is raised in an audit or by a customer. How test results feed back. Defects and risks detected are prioritised by severity and reflected in prompt revisions, additional output filters, and review of the intended scope of use. After remediation we re-test and check whether the same weakness exists in other features or other products. Distinguishing types of AI system. Generative AI features are managed on the assumption that outputs of external foundation models may contain bias or hallucination, so controls centre on verification: retrieval grounding with source citation, output filtering, and a human confirmation step, with the original text displayed by default and always retrievable (our "safety net structure"). Agentic AI systems that plan or act to a partial extent are under evaluation.Both categories are managed on the premise of a human-in-the-loop, in which a healthcare professional or a user makes the final decision. Because an error in the medical domain can be irreversible, any future agentic capability would additionally require an explicit boundary of autonomous action and a human decision point before any action affecting a patient or a medical record.

• Data minimisation and anonymisation: personal and sensitive data is anonymised or pseudonymised before entering AI pipelines; testing uses anonymised or synthetic data only.
• Encryption in transit and at rest for all data stores and AI-related data flows.
• Access control: role-based access, least-privilege, and secrets management for model provider credentials.
• Provider data-flow governance: for each project we document what data reaches which model provider under what contractual terms, and select providers/configurations with no training on customer data; where client requirements demand it, we deploy on-premise or private-cloud inference.
• Disclosure prevention at the application layer: retrieval components are scoped per-user/per-role so the system cannot surface documents the requesting user is not authorised to see; agent tool access is similarly permission-scoped; outputs in sensitive contexts pass human review before external use.
• Logging and audit trails of AI interactions, retained under defined retention policies.
• Contractual safeguards: NDAs and data-processing agreements with clients define confidentiality obligations covering AI components.

Our organization applies risk management during the complete AI system lifecycle.
The AI Lab designs, tests, validates, documents, and monitors AI systems. Business, Quality, Security, and Data Protection stakeholders review risks in their areas of responsibility. The Digital Committee performs an independent review of significant AI use cases before deployment. Significant risks can be escalated to the Digital Committee for additional review and decision.
Our AI systems use Microsoft technologies, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, Azure AI services, Power Automate, and Microsoft Graph connectors. We use Microsoft evaluation and observability capabilities to assess quality, grounding, hallucination rates, prompt injection resistance, indirect prompt injection resistance, output safety, content filtering effectiveness, agent tool usage, performance, and reliability. We also use workflow run history, error logs, conversation logs (when enabled), audit records, and operational monitoring data to support governance, traceability, and operational oversight.
Before deployment, each AI system undergoes risk assessment, testing, evaluation, validation, security review, privacy review, and documentation review. Higher-risk systems receive additional controls and oversight. Agentic AI systems receive additional review of autonomy, orchestration logic, authorization limits, tool access, multi-agent interactions, and human oversight mechanisms.
After deployment, the organization monitors evaluation results, system performance, execution logs, workflow histories, error records, conversation logs, and incident reports. Each issue receives a risk score. The risk score determines the escalation path and remediation timeline. Corrective actions must be completed within defined timelines ranging from 2 to 30 days. 
The organization reviews its AI governance practices regularly and whenever significant events occur, which in practice has meant every quarter! Risk assessments, evaluation results, and controls are updated as required

MGOIT employs a proactive, multi-layered risk assessment approach to detect and mitigate vulnerabilities, emerging risks, and potential misuse across the AI lifecycle. Our framework integrates continuous monitoring, automated safeguards, and human oversight to ensure AI systems remain secure, ethical, and aligned with global regulations.
1. Risk Identification & Vulnerability Assessment
🔹 Threat Modeling & Risk Mapping – We systematically identify vulnerabilities at each AI lifecycle stage (data collection, model training, deployment, and monitoring).
🔹 Adversarial Testing & Red-Teaming – AI models undergo simulated attacks to assess weaknesses against adversarial inputs, bias exploitation, and security breaches.
🔹 Bias & Fairness Audits – Automated fairness testing combined with human review ensures that AI decisions remain unbiased and equitable.
🔹 Regulatory Compliance Checks – We align with EU AI Act, GDPR, and other global AI governance frameworks to mitigate regulatory risks.
2. Incident Detection & Emerging Risk Monitoring
🔹 Automated Risk Detection – Real-time anomaly detection tools flag unexpected behaviors, drifts, and performance deviations in AI models.
🔹 Human-in-the-Loop Oversight – Continuous expert review helps validate critical AI outputs, preventing misuse and reinforcing ethical decision-making.
🔹 Explainability & Transparency Tools – We implement SHAP, LIME, and custom explainability models to ensure AI reasoning can be audited and justified.
🔹 Privacy-Preserving AI – Differential privacy and federated learning techniques reduce data exposure risks while maintaining model accuracy.
3. Misuse Prevention & Risk Mitigation
🔹 Access Control & Governance – AI systems incorporate robust authentication, monitoring, and role-based access to prevent unauthorized manipulation.
🔹 Ethical AI Guidelines & User Training – We provide clear AI usage policies and educate end-users on responsible AI interactions.
🔹 Continuous Model Auditing & Iterative Improvements – AI models are routinely retrained and audited to minimize drift and emerging vulnerabilities.
Commitment to Responsible AI
By integrating these best practices, MGOIT ensures that AI solutions remain trustworthy, transparent, and resilient while adapting to the dynamic landscape of AI risk management.

Jus Mundi uses a risk-based approval process before deploying AI systems. Decision authority depends on the risk level and involves the Product and Engineering owners, with Security, Legal/DPO, and AI governance review where confidentiality, privacy, compliance, customer impact, or service integrity may be affected.
Before release, the team reviews the intended use, data involved, vendor or model assessment, security and privacy risks, testing results, output quality, robustness, misuse scenarios, access controls, monitoring, and compliance requirements. Deployment is allowed only when performance is acceptable for the intended use, critical risks are mitigated, and the residual risk is within the organization’s risk appetite.
Higher-risk or customer-facing systems require additional sign-off and may be escalated to governance bodies. Required safeguards may include human oversight, access controls, data minimization, logging, user guidance, source attribution, monitoring, incident response, rollback mechanisms, and phased deployment. For agentic AI, Jus Mundi applies stricter controls on autonomy, permissions, approval gates, audit trails, and the ability to suspend unsafe behavior.

Our organization integrates AI risk management into its overall governance framework.
The AI Lab provides technical, operational, and governance expertise. The AI Lab performs risk assessments, testing, validation, documentation, monitoring, and recommendations for AI systems.
Business stakeholders, Data Protection representatives, Quality Assurance personnel, Information Security personnel, and subject matter experts provide advisory review within their areas of responsibility.
The Digital Committee performs an independent governance review of significant AI use cases. The Digital Committee has decision-making authority for approval, rejection, escalation, or the application of additional controls before deployment.
Final accountability for AI risk-related decisions remains with the designated business owner and the organization's governance structure. Deployment cannot proceed without the required reviews and approvals.
AI governance policies, risk assessments, controls, and operating procedures are reviewed on a regular basis and whenever significant events occur, in practice this has been every quarter.
Review and update triggers can include:
Security incidents.
Privacy incidents.
Compliance findings.
Regulatory or legal changes.
Significant model or system performance issues.
Material changes to AI system functionality.
New AI capabilities or agentic features.
Newly identified risks.
Model expiry or retirement events.
When a review identifies new or increased risk, the organization updates the risk assessment and determines the required corrective actions. Corrective actions can include additional testing, additional monitoring, updated controls, deployment restrictions, model replacement, or model retirement.
For higher-risk AI systems, including agentic AI systems, the organization applies additional governance, review, monitoring, and human oversight requirements before and after deployment.

Salesforce does have formal programs to incentivize the disclosure of AI risks, vulnerabilities, and incidents. These efforts are primarily centralized through our Bug Bounty Program and our Office of Ethical and Humane Use, which have evolved to specifically address the unique risks of generative and agentic AI.
1. The Bug Bounty Program (Financial Incentives) - Bug Bounty Program  
Salesforce operates one of the most active bug bounty programs in the tech industry, which explicitly includes AI-specific testing.
Expansion to AI: The program incentivizes ethical hackers to identify not just traditional security flaws, but also AI bias, prompt injection, and harmful model behaviors.
Incentives: Salesforce has paid out over $23 million to date through its bug bounty network. In 2023 alone, they paid over $3 million to roughly 650 researchers.
Focus on Agentic AI: With the rise of autonomous agents (like Agentforce), the program now specifically targets systemic vulnerabilities where AI might autonomously make incorrect or insecure decisions without human input.
2. Responsible Disclosure & Ethical Reporting
Beyond financial rewards for hackers, Salesforce has structured frameworks for reporting and transparency:
HAIP Reporting Framework: Salesforce participates in the OECD’s Reporting Framework for AI System Developers. This involves documenting and disclosing how they evaluate models against trust and safety metrics such as privacy, robustness, and bias.
Adversarial Testing: When AI models score poorly on safety metrics, Salesforce incentivizes internal and external teams to use red teaming (adversarial testing) to find and report how those risks manifest in practice.
Model Cards: The use of Model Cards for our predictive and generative AI to disclose known risks, ethical considerations, and appropriate use cases to the public and our customers.
3. The Einstein Trust Layer
While not a reporting program in the traditional sense, this architecture acts as a systemic catch-all for vulnerabilities:
Feedback Loops: The Trust Layer includes mechanisms for users to report toxic or incorrect AI outputs, which are then used to refine the models.
Data Masking & Audit Trails: It provides a systemic disclosure mechanism by creating an audit trail of all AI interactions, allowing organizations to monitor and report incidents of data exposure or policy violations internally.
4. Vulnerability Disclosure Policy (VDP) - Vulnerability Reporting 
Salesforce maintains a Vulnerability Disclosure Policy that provides a safe harbor for researchers. This program ensures that individuals who discover and report systemic AI vulnerabilities in good faith are not met with legal action, provided they follow the company's disclosure guidelines.

TELUS has a dedicated Data & Trust Office with over 50 privacy, data governance and data ethics professionals.  This includes an in-house Data Ethicist and resources trained in ethical machine learning techniques. Team members participate in external training, including the International Association of Privacy Professionals’ AI Governance Professional certification.  TELUS is a foundational sponsor of this program. TELUS also offers OCAP® (Ownership, Control, Access, and Possession) training for TELUS team members who support data privacy, ethics, governance and AI in order to deepen understanding of Indigenous data sovereignty.
Across the organization, team members are appointed as Data Stewards by their business unit for their in-depth knowledge of their team’s data uses and the intended strategy for that data. TELUS has over 500 data stewards who participate in a customized certification training program which equips and empowers the responsible use of AI through data privacy, security and governance.  Across the AI lifecycle, business and technology teams are active participants in the identification, mitigation and acceptance of risk when using data with the support of TELUS’ data governance processes.  In addition, certified Data Stewards pursue additional external training and certification from the International Association of Privacy Professionals.  
The Data & Trust Office also runs a data and AI literacy campaign for all team members to better understand both the opportunity of data and AI, but also the governance policies and risk management practices.  This included partnering with Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (CIFAR) on the promotion of the Destination.AI literacy training program, and organizations like Microsoft and Google to share their learning resources. 
Immersive training also takes place through our TELUS Purple Team.  We believe responsible use of AI requires input from a diverse set of voices.  Through our purple teaming exercises, we invite any and all team members to participate in a collaborative exercise to identify weaknesses, vulnerabilities, and gaps in generative AI systems through adversarial testing and address them with relevant mitigations. In addition to the participation from the Software Developers, Data Scientists and AI Engineers, it emphasizes the participation of diverse individuals with varying expertise and technical literacy to gain comprehensive insights into the system's shortcomings and how real users may interact with the solution. Before sessions begin, participants receive training on AI fundamentals and potential risks, ensuring everyone can contribute meaningfully regardless of technical background. Beyond finding vulnerabilities, these hands-on sessions help participants understand how AI works, how it can fail, and why responsible AI development matters. This creates a ripple effect of AI literacy and awareness throughout TELUS, building a more informed workforce that can better navigate an AI-enabled future.

Malt manages AI-related incidents through its general incident management policy, which is integrated with Malt’ information security management system (ie. tracking system), the information security policy and the data breach policy. Every incident is recorded in a live incident document which includes a root cause analysis report. Once the incident is resolved, a post-incident analysis is conducted to further understand root causes, control gaps and measures required to prevent recurrence.
Escalation thresholds are based on severity and impact. Escalation may involve the system owner, ML or engineering teams, information security team, the DPO, legal, senior management. A critical impact on users, legal obligations, finances, productivity or reputation may trigger escalation to the executive committee. Incidents are shared with external parties—such as regulatory authorities and impacted users—when legally mandated or to prevent unintended outcomes.
Incident records and the personal-data breach register are used for audits, accountability, trend analysis, risk-register updates, control improvements, training and future deployment decisions. Major incidents, material system changes, new vulnerabilities, significant evaluation findings and regulatory developments trigger an ad hoc review of the relevant AI risk assessment and controls by the AI deployment committee.

Microsoft applies a comprehensive and layered risk management approach across the AI lifecycle, grounded in the Responsible AI Standard and supported by scenario-specific requirements for particular technologies, capabilities, and use cases. This approach is designed to uphold Microsoft’s AI principles consistently across the development lifecycle by defining policies, assigning roles and responsibilities, enabling proactive risk management, and establishing processes that reinforce responsible AI by design.
How the practices operate together.  Microsoft draws on the Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Consistent with this approach, teams identify reasonably foreseeable risks and benefits; use red teaming, evaluations, and other measurement methods to assess risks and the effectiveness of mitigations; implement layered technical and operational safeguards; and document the evidence supporting deployment decisions. Measurement and mitigation are iterative: evaluation results inform mitigations, and systems are reassessed following mitigation to determine whether residual risks have been appropriately addressed.
The Responsible AI Standard serves as Microsoft’s internal playbook for building AI systems in alignment with its AI principles. Core requirements apply across Microsoft’s AI technologies, while additional requirements and review processes are applied according to the technology’s capabilities, intended uses, and risk profile. These include requirements for generative AI systems and models; the Frontier Governance Framework for advanced model capabilities that could pose national security or at-scale public safety risks; and the Sensitive Uses and Emerging Technologies program for higher-impact uses and novel technologies or risks.
Pre-deployment review connects these practices and supports consistent release decisions. Product teams document how applicable requirements have been met, including the risks identified, evaluations undertaken, mitigations applied, and any residual risks. Relevant experts review higher-risk or higher-impact uses and generative AI releases, and teams may be required to conduct further evaluation or implement additional safeguards before release. Depending on the risk profile, safeguards may include post-training interventions, system prompts, input and output classifiers, human review, transparency documentation, user feedback mechanisms, and phased or staged release. Post-deployment monitoring, incident reporting, user feedback, and real-world deployment experience then provide signals that can prompt reassessment and feed into improvements to products, engineering practices, and policy.
Governance and escalation. Product teams manage risk for the technologies they build. The Office of Responsible AI maintains the Responsible AI Standard and leads the development of new policies and guidance, informed by regulatory developments, pre-deployment reviews, red teaming, product roadmaps, research, ongoing monitoring, and incident response. The Responsible AI engineering function develops supporting tools and technical guidance so that policy requirements can be integrated into engineering workflows. Deployment of a frontier model rests with Executive Officers or their delegates, as described in our response to question 2.A. After release, escalation follows the severity assigned under the AI Security and Safety Bug Bar (see 23.A). Oversight structures, including the Responsible AI Council and reporting to the Board, are described in our response to question 21.A.
Review and updates. Microsoft reviews and updates its responsible AI policies, practices, tools, and individual risk assessments on an ongoing and event-driven basis. Relevant triggers include new or materially changed system capabilities; major product or deployment changes; evaluation, red-teaming, or monitoring results; reported vulnerabilities or incidents; evidence from real-world use and user feedback; advances in risk measurement or mitigation; research and horizon-scanning findings; and changes in applicable laws, standards, or regulatory expectations.
The Frontier Governance Framework includes additional review points for models within its scope. Leading-indicator assessments are conducted during pre-training, after pre-training, after post-training, and before deployment, and at least every six months thereafter for models within scope. A further capability assessment is conducted where leading indicators warrant deeper inspection, with subsequent assessments triggered by material changes to a deployed model’s risk profile. Microsoft also commits to an explicit discussion at least every twelve months on how the FGF should be improved, with material revisions published within 30 days of adoption.
Generative and agentic AI. Microsoft formalized specific internal requirements for generative AI systems in 2023 and has continued to update them as capabilities, risks, and regulatory requirements evolve. Generative AI releases are subject to pre-deployment review, red teaming, evaluation, mitigation, and documentation requirements tailored to their capabilities and deployment context. Agentic AI requires additional attention because systems may connect multiple models, tools, data sources, permissions, and memory, and may take actions with increasing autonomy over time. Microsoft therefore addresses agentic risks through system-level threat modelling, evaluation of autonomy, planning and tool use, controls governing access and permissions, and safeguards designed around the system’s deployment context. Where agentic capabilities may indicate advanced autonomy or other tracked high-risk capabilities, the Frontier Governance Framework provides for leading-indicator assessment, deeper capability assessment, proportionate mitigation, and risk-informed deployment decisions.

When developing and operating AI models and services, we consider attacks on AI systems, such as data poisoning and prompt injection in Gen AI, and take measures such as risk verification, the introduction of protection functions, and appropriate access control. In addition, the department in charge of AI safety and security conducts general security and safety-related tests to evaluate the suitability of models and systems.
Cybersecurity risks are assessed based on industry standards, guidelines, and frameworks, such as the NIST SP-800 series, Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 for LLM, and MITRE Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems (ATLAS). In addition to implementing all general cybersecurity policies, we also establish AI-specific policies to ensure secure development and operations.
In the department that oversees cyber security, we manage vulnerabilities related to the services provided by the Rakuten Group. All vulnerabilities detected during development, testing and operation, as well as vulnerability information received from other stakeholders, are registered in our vulnerability management database and managed accordingly. 
The Rakuten Group is registered as a product developer in the Early Warning Partnership operated by the Japan Computer Emergency Response Team / Coordination Center (JPCERT/CC), which is operated by the Information-Technology Promotion Agency, Japan (IPA), and we work closely with them.
At a minimum, reviews are conducted once a year. In addition to the regular review process, we incorporate updates based on lessons learned from our incident response activities and make adjustments to our security testing methodologies as new techniques are disclosed.
We use a cloud access security broker (CASB) to monitor for threats caused by internal misconduct or human error. In addition, we have set up the Rakuten Hotline, which is an internal and external whistleblowing hotline that all Rakuten Group employees can use to consult or report on any behavior that violates or may violate laws, corporate ethics, or internal regulations, regardless of whether they are full-time, contract, part-time, or other type of employee.
In operating this hotline, and through similar whistleblowing protections in other jurisdictions, we protect the confidentiality of those who consult or report to the hotline, and prohibit and protect against any disadvantageous treatment of those who do so in accordance with applicable laws.

Decision authority. Release of an AI feature is decided by the responsible product team on the basis of a cross-product review by the Trust & Safety Team. Risk assessment is performed by dedicated specialists independent of the development and business units in order to ensure objectivity. Where a material concern remains, the decision escalates to the Risk and Compliance Committee (legal, security, public relations and other functions), which deliberates the trade-off between AI utilization and risk together with the Generative AI Promotion Team. This two-layer structure is featured as an advanced case (Column 11) in the Appendix to the METI/MIC AI Guidelines for Business (Ver. 1.1). Evidence and criteria required. Review and approval gates are applied at each stage. At the planning stage we assess the use case, the users, data sensitivity, and impacts on medical safety, privacy and security. Before release, the evidence required against defined test criteria comprises: functional testing; medical review by physicians of clinical accuracy; sample evaluation of generative AI outputs, including hallucination and source attribution; security assessment, including prompt injection; privacy review covering the scope of data sent to external foundation models and retention in logs; legal and regulatory compliance review (Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Act, Medical Practitioners Act, Act on the Protection of Personal Information, and the Two Guidelines from Three Ministries); and fairness review across disease, age, sex, expression of symptoms, and region or access to healthcare. Independent external assurance is used for information security, through ISMS (ISO/IEC 27001:2022) audit and security assessment. Contextual caveats in interpreting risk evaluation metric results. Evaluation results are read as conditional rather than absolute. Sample evaluation of generative outputs is not exhaustive, so a passing result is not evidence of the absence of hallucination. Benchmark and test-set performance does not transfer directly to real clinical language, which includes dialects, abbreviations and non-standard medical terminology. Because our products are built on external foundation models, results are valid only for the model and version tested, and are re-examined when the model, version or data integration method changes. For these reasons we do not treat any single metric as a sole release criterion, and human confirmation is retained as the controlling safeguard. Approvals and sign-offs. Confirmation of conformity with our quality standards by the Trust & Safety Team is required before release. Deployment at a medical institution additionally requires confirmation of that customer's security and operational requirements under contract. A fresh security review is triggered by material changes to external foundation models, cloud services or data integration methods, and by amendments to applicable laws or guidelines. Safeguards required to move into deployment. Prompt and guardrail design with input and output filtering; a human confirmation step for any output that materially affects a care decision; the "safety net structure", in which the original text is displayed by default and can always be referenced; access rights restricted so that highly confidential data of a medical institution is accessible only to that institution; cautionary notices in wording and UI; operating procedures and customer training; and continuous log and error monitoring after release. Where risk warrants it, we limit the scope of provision or release in phases. Where material risk remains, we postpone or do not release.

Evaluation results are shared with stakeholders according to the purpose, risk level, and applicable legal or regulatory requirements.
Internally, evaluation results are reviewed by the AI Lab, business owners, Quality Assurance, Information Security, Data Protection, and the Digital Committee when required.
In France, information related to AI deployments is also shared with employee representative bodies when required by applicable legal obligations, including consultation and information processes involving the Comité Social et Économique (CSE).
Evaluation results support deployment decisions, risk assessments, corrective actions, monitoring activities, and governance reviews.
The organization provides both technical and non-technical summaries. Technical reports are used for validation, governance, and audit purposes. Plain-language summaries are used when communicating with business stakeholders, employees, management, and other non-technical audiences.
Selected results, lessons learned, and governance practices can also be shared with customers, partners, professional networks, industry forums, academic collaborators, conference audiences, or regulatory stakeholders when appropriate.
The organization shares information in a manner that protects confidential information, personal data, intellectual property, and applicable regulatory obligations.

Karavela has not yet deployed an AI model or system. Our models are currently developed and evaluated in a research setting, and a formal deployment approval process has not yet been established.
 
Before any deployment, we expect decision authority to rest with company leadership, informed by scientific and technical leads and, where relevant, clinical, legal and data-protection expertise. Amazon takes a lifecycle-based approach to managing the risks of AI, including potential risks that can arise from misuse of our advanced AI models. Our strategy is grounded in pre-deployment evaluation and post-deployment monitoring, with particular focus on three critical risk domains: Chemical, Biological, Radiological & Nuclear (CBRN), Offensive Cyber Operations, and Automated AI R&D.
 
Our pre-deployment evaluations combine automated benchmarks with human-centric assessments, including expert red-teaming and multi-agent stress tests. For example, our recent Amazon Nova Premier evaluation incorporated both reproducible automated testing and independent verification from specialized firms like Nemesys Insights for CBRN assessments and METR for automated AI R&D evaluations. These comprehensive assessments help our models remain within defined safety thresholds before release.
 
Post-deployment, we maintain continuous monitoring through automated detection systems and dynamic content filters that protect against misuse while preserving model functionality. For details about our security and privacy protections, please see our previous responses and the "Security" section of our AWS AI Service Cards for Amazon Nova models.
 
For more detailed information about our approach to specific risk domains and evaluation methodologies, please see our Frontier Model Safety Framework and Amazon Nova Premier Evaluation report.

Governance framework.  Microsoft embeds AI risk management through a layered governance framework combining company-wide requirements, specialist review, executive decision-making and Board oversight. The Responsible AI Standard translates Microsoft’s Responsible AI principles into requirements for teams developing and deploying AI models, platform services and applications. The Office of Responsible AI (ORA), led by the Chief Responsible AI Officer, manages this framework, defines roles and responsibilities, establishes governance processes and provides guidance on legal and regulatory requirements. Day-to-day implementation is supported by engineering partners and the Responsible AI Governance Community embedded across product groups.
Specialist and advisory review. Specialist review complements requirements. Under the Sensitive Uses program, ORA works with product engineering and customer and partner solutions teams where foreseeable use or misuse meets Sensitive Use criteria, with reviews resulting in additional requirements where appropriate. ORA also provides early guidance on emerging capabilities and risks not yet addressed by formal policy, while Microsoft Research and external subject-matter experts provide research-informed advisory input. For qualifying generative AI products and features, ORA, a responsible AI engineering team, and experts from the Responsible AI Governance Community facilitate centralized or expert-led review processes. These review mechanisms operate at scale: between July 2025 and June 2026, Microsoft conducted nearly 2,500 generative AI product and feature reviews and more than 450 Sensitive Use reviews.
Executive oversight and decision-making. At executive level, the Responsible AI Council, co-led by Microsoft’s Vice Chair and President Brad Smith and the Chief Technology Officer and Executive Vice President of AI Kevin Scott, meets quarterly and oversees company-wide progress. It includes Corporate Vice Presidents from across the business, supported by division-level leaders responsible for operationalizing the responsible AI program. At Board level, Microsoft’s responsible AI leaders engage regularly with the Board of Directors through internal enterprise risk management reviews as well as engagement with the Environmental, Social and Public Policy Committee. Under the Frontier Governance Framework, for frontier models, the Executive Officers responsible for Microsoft’s AI governance program, or their delegates, make the final decision on whether to approve the recommendation for secure and trustworthy deployment. Along with other responsible AI policies and programs, the Frontier Governance Framework is subject to internal audit and Board oversight.
Review and adaptation. Policies and requirements are reviewed and updated on an ongoing basis in response to technological developments, regulatory changes, identified risks and incidents, lessons from after-action reviews and implementation feedback. The Responsible AI Standard has been progressively updated as AI capabilities, risks and regulatory expectations have evolved. Most recently, it was re-engineered to include dedicated Developer and Deployer Chapters and to distinguish core requirements from scenario-specific requirements. As part of this work, Microsoft analysed more than 100 enacted and proposed laws and refreshed its process for continuous regulatory analysis and adaptation. The Frontier Governance Framework also requires an explicit review at least every twelve months. Changes to practices are reviewed by the Chief Responsible AI Officer before adoption, and material revisions are published within 30 days of adoption.

Plan and design: We identify how a system is intended to be used and what could go wrong, then use that assessment to decide which tests and safeguards are needed.
Collect and process data: We select, prepare and filter training data, applying relevant privacy protections and controls over where data comes from.
Build, integrate and interpret model: We test the model as it is developed and use the findings to improve its behavior and relevant protections.
Verify and validate: We examine what the system can do and safeguards’ effectiveness, using internal automated and human testing and relevant input from outside experts.
Deploy: We review the evidence and the risks that remain after safeguards are applied before deciding whether and how to release the system, which may include phased deployment to understand potential risk among a smaller audience before broadening access.
Operate and monitor: We monitor for misuse and incidents after release and use what we learn to improve safeguards and future assessments.
Evaluations are performed at multiple points throughout the AI lifecycle to ensure models are safe, effective, and align with OpenAI's objectives. In the pre-development phase, we begin with an initial risk assessment to identify potential hazards and define safety objectives, establishing a foundation for informed and responsible development. During the development phase, models undergo iterative testing to refine safety and performance as the model evolves. Before deployment, in the pre-deployment phase, we conduct a range of safety and capability evaluations, as described in our Preparedness Framework. In the deployment phase, we implement system safeguards to prevent harm and monitoring to detect unexpected behaviors or misuse, and we perform post-deployment evaluations using real-world feedback and performance data to identify emerging risks. Finally, in the post-deployment and maintenance phase, we update our evaluations and safeguards based on new misuse patterns, identified incidents, and advances in research.
We embed security controls into infrastructure and model development, and use adversarial testing, monitoring and incident review to improve them. Our work on long-horizon models has also shown why individual action checks alone can be insufficient: a sequence of seemingly acceptable actions can cross a user’s intended boundary.
Significant releases, material evaluation findings, incidents, emerging abuse patterns and changes in applicable requirements can trigger reviews and updates. Findings may change evaluations, model behavior, safeguards, access conditions or monitoring. The Safety Advisory Group advises OpenAI leadership on preparedness decisions, and relevant research, safety, security, product, legal and policy teams contribute according to their responsibilities. An explanation of the safety work for a model is published in a system card when the model is released to general availability.
Findings from internal use, evaluations and incident investigations inform our alignment work, security controls and decisions about whether work can proceed. Our September 25, 2026 report provides a further example of how incident findings change safeguards and research decisions. An internal research model accessed an external chatbot through insufficient DNS filtering in its training sandbox. Monitoring detected the behavior, but the investigation also identified gaps in detection and operational response. We stopped the affected training run and added blocking controls at two independent layers. At time of publication, training, evaluation and tool-using inference for our most capable models were paused pending validation that the gap was resolved and additional red teaming. We also committed to beginning a fresh training run with additional alignment improvements rather than resuming training of the affected model.

Our organization uses a defined governance process before deployment of an AI model or system.
The AI Lab designs, develops, tests, and validates the solution.
Business stakeholders, Data Protection, Quality Assurance, and Security representatives review risks in their areas of responsibility.
The Digital Committee performs an independent review before deployment. The Digital Committee has authority to approve, reject, or request additional controls for significant AI use cases.
Before deployment, the project team must provide evidence for:
Functional performance.
Security controls.
Privacy controls.
System robustness and reliability.
Compliance with applicable requirements.
Risk assessment results.
Test, evaluation, validation, and verification activities.
Known limitations and residual risks.
Risk evaluation results must be interpreted in the context of the intended use, operating environment, data quality, available controls, and identified limitations. Risk metrics alone do not determine deployment approval.
The following approvals can be required before deployment:
Business Owner approval.
Data Protection approval, when applicable.
Quality Assurance approval, when applicable.
Digital Committee approval for significant AI use cases.
Before deployment, the organization must implement appropriate safeguards. These safeguards can include:
Technical and procedural risk mitigations.
Access controls and authorization limits.
Human oversight measures.
Monitoring and logging controls.
Incident management procedures.
Usage restrictions and operational guardrails.
Additional testing and validation activities.
The organization can restrict deployment scope or delay deployment if the identified controls are not sufficient to reduce risk to an acceptable level.
After deployment, the organization continues monitoring activities and reviews the solution regularly to verify compliance, performance, and effectiveness of controls.

Jus Mundi does not currently rely on a single quantitative threshold to determine when an AI-related risk becomes “unreasonable.” Instead, severe AI risks are assessed through a risk-based governance process aligned with the organization’s role as a legal intelligence and technology provider, and with its broader security, privacy, compliance and AI governance frameworks. The most relevant references are ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 27001, the EU AI Act, OECD AI Principles, data protection requirements, and internal information security and risk management policies.
A risk may be considered unreasonable or intolerable when, after considering available mitigations, it could create a severe impact on individuals, clients, the legal process, confidentiality, security, regulatory compliance, or the integrity of Jus Mundi’s services. Examples include: unauthorized disclosure or processing of confidential legal or personal data; AI outputs that could materially mislead users in legal research or decision-making if presented without appropriate caveats or human review; system behavior that could compromise the availability, integrity or security of the platform; discriminatory or unfair outputs in sensitive contexts; or autonomous actions performed without adequate authorization, traceability or human oversight.
In practice, Jus Mundi evaluates these risks using decision criteria such as severity of potential harm, likelihood, scale of exposure, sensitivity of the data involved, reversibility of harm, detectability, regulatory impact, customer impact, and the effectiveness of controls. Risks that remain high or critical after mitigation require escalation to the relevant governance bodies and accountable functions, including Security, Legal/DPO, Product, Engineering and AI governance stakeholders. Deployment may be blocked, delayed, limited to a controlled environment, or subject to additional safeguards where residual risk is not acceptable.
Mitigations are graduated according to the capability and risk profile of the AI system. Lower-risk use cases may require standard controls such as documentation, user guidance, access control, logging, human review and monitoring. Higher-risk use cases may require enhanced review, security and privacy assessments, vendor due diligence, model or application testing, stricter access restrictions, output validation, contractual safeguards, phased deployment, incident response procedures and formal approval before release.
For generative AI, Jus Mundi pays particular attention to hallucination, explainability, source attribution, confidentiality, prompt/input handling, copyright and data protection risks, and user reliance on AI-generated outputs. For agentic AI or tool-using systems, additional scrutiny is applied to autonomy, permissions, ability to take actions, access to sensitive systems or data, auditability, rollback capacity, and human-in-the-loop controls. Agentic capabilities would be restricted or prohibited where they could perform high-impact actions without appropriate authorization, monitoring, and intervention mechanisms.

Organization-wide measures. We operate a risk-based security program with periodic risk assessments reported to senior management, and hold ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certifications alongside annual SOC 2 Type II examinations (reports via trust.anthropic.com). We maintain a threat-actor register and externally validated threat models spanning endpoint, supply-chain, physical, cloud, privilege-escalation and exfiltration vectors, and red-team AI-specific risks such as prompt injection. Baseline controls include multi-factor authentication and least-privilege, role-based access; managed-device access controls, endpoint detection and response, and application allowlisting on workstations; encryption at rest and in transit; network segmentation and data-loss controls; centralized logging with automated anomaly alerting; peer review and automated security analysis of code; continuous vulnerability scanning, risk-based remediation, annual external penetration testing, a public Responsible Disclosure Policy and bug bounties; layered physical security at our facilities and review of cloud service providers' independently audited data-center controls; and incident-response and business-continuity plans with escalation procedures for high-severity incidents, tested annually.
Measures specific to particularly sensitive AI assets. Our most sensitive AI assets are the weights of our most capable models; related training data and source code are restricted on a least-privilege, business-need basis. Weights additionally receive the ASL-3 protections our Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) commits us to maintain or improve, designed to protect against most non-state attackers: multi-party, time-limited authorization using hardware security keys; device authorization limiting weight-system access to approved managed devices; egress bandwidth controls making large-scale exfiltration more time-consuming and detectable; cloud storage restrictions designed to prevent weights being written outside our security perimeter; network-source restrictions on privileged resources; additional review and commit-integrity requirements for critical repositories; and encryption, access logging and automated detection of unauthorized weight access or movement. Third-party partners hosting these models must implement equivalent security controls.
Personnel and insider risk (organization-wide). We apply pre-employment background checks where legally permissible; confidentiality agreements binding employees and contractor personnel before access is provisioned; security-awareness training at hire and annually, supplemented by AI-incident-response training for relevant staff; and a formal insider-risk program with internal monitoring, documented investigation and escalation procedures, and confidential and anonymous reporting channels, including RSP-noncompliance reporting with protection from retaliation.
Assurance. We publish RSP Risk Reports every three to six months and a Frontier Safety Roadmap of security goals; our Frontier Compliance Framework and "Activating ASL-3 Protections" report give more detail.
We run a dedicated insider-risk program under the security standards in our Responsible Scaling Policy: role-proportionate pre-employment verification, least-privilege access to model weights and sensitive assets with logging and monitoring, mandatory security training at hire and annually, and defined escalation channels to our Insider Risk and Security teams, including anonymous RSP noncompliance reporting. See our ASL-3 activation report and Trust Center.

Question 12 — vulnerability management
OpenAI receives vulnerability reports through its security and safety bounty programs and provides an encrypted channel for reporting security incidents. Its disclosure policy also describes coordination for vulnerabilities found in third-party software and its role as a CVE Numbering Authority. 
For covered frontier systems, security assessments include red teaming, penetration testing and vulnerability scanning.
Question 13 — post-deployment practices
OpenAI disallows the use of our models and tools for certain activities and content, as outlined in our terms and usage policies. These policies are designed to prohibit the use of our models and tools in ways that cause individual or societal harm. We periodically update these policies in response to new risks and new information on how our models are being used. Access to and use of our models are also subject to OpenAI’s Terms of Use and our Business Terms. We employ a combination of guardrails, tools, policies, and processes to detect and enforce against abuse of our models. In addition to usage policies, we employ automated systems (for example, our Moderation API) and AI-powered tools to detect and prevent harmful content, human reviewers and expert investigators to conduct detailed investigations of model behavior and platform abuse, and external input to help our teams iterate on and regularly improve our moderation, detection, disruption, and enforcement capabilities. We publish information related to our post-deployment monitoring, mitigation and enforcement activities.
We build robust monitoring systems to detect potential model misalignment. We view model alignment as the primary lever to prevent potential misaligned behavior from our models. However, monitoring provides broad visibility into frontier model behavior, illuminating opportunities to further improve alignment and safety. This serves as an additional layer of protection against misaligned behavior that is detected.
Addressing vulnerabilities, incidents, emerging risks and misuse often requires participation from a number of teams across the company, including where applicable, teams responsible for research; safety and alignment; product; user or customer relationships and support; intelligence, investigations and teams supporting scaled detection and enforcement; security; policy teams; global affairs; legal and privacy; and communications.
Post-deployment, we rely on monitoring, user feedback, periodic security evaluations, and incident reporting to track risk emergence over time. Material findings can be fed back into model update cycles, safety classifiers, or policy adjustments.
Questions 14 and 14A — agentic systems and controls
Yes. Some of our products can perform supported tasks using tools and a cloud browser, including reading websites and completing multi-step workflows. It pauses when it needs user input, sign-in, or confirmation. Cloud browser documentation.
We design controls to help users remain in charge of an agent’s work. In our agentic products, users can manage website permissions, review consequential actions, and take over the cloud browser. OpenAI tests for prompt injection, phishing, and unintended actions, among other things.
We also train and test the agent to resist prompt injection: attempts to make it follow malicious instructions hidden in material it encounters, such as a webpage. Monitoring helps us detect and respond to these attacks. Secure browser takeover allows users to enter credentials without exposing those inputs to the model. Together, these measures address risks that arise when an agent uses outside information or works through services where the user is signed in.
Additionally, we train the model to be aligned with human intentions, and monitor for misalignment issues. This monitoring helps us detect and respond to issues as they arise in internal and external deployment, allowing us to iterate on further safeguard and evaluation development.

Excelya invests in research and practical initiatives that support responsible use of AI in regulated environments.
A major area of focus is Human-in-the-Loop (HITL), professional judgement, and human oversight in Medical Affairs, Medical Information, pharmacovigilance, regulatory, and compliance workflows. Our work examines what professionals need in order to exercise meaningful judgement when reviewing AI-assisted outputs, including access to evidence, decision authority, escalation pathways, and the ability to challenge or reject AI-generated content.
We are particularly interested in situations where individuals remain accountable for decisions supported by AI. Current work explores how organizations can prevent oversight from becoming a simple approval step and instead support genuine review, critical thinking, and professional responsibility.
Research topics include professional judgement, cognitive workload, automation bias, trust in AI systems, human-AI collaboration, auditability, and governance. The objective is to develop practical approaches that organizations can use to evaluate whether Human-in-the-Loop controls are effective in real-world regulated workflows.
We intend to share selected findings through scientific and professional channels. Planned outputs include a potential manuscript for Therapeutic Innovation & Regulatory Science (TIRS) and conference presentations or posters at events such as AISEAI. The goal is to contribute practical evidence and governance guidance for organizations that deploy AI in regulated environments.

Malt distinguishes between recommendation systems, generative AI and agentic AI. Generative systems receive additional controls for prompt and output security, factuality, privacy, provider processing and human review. Agentic systems, where applicable, require additional safeguards such as least-privilege access, approved tool lists, action limits, human confirmation for consequential actions and an effective interruption or shutdown mechanism. 
The lifecycle process is reviewed and updated under three circumstances: (1) when a new system version or model iteration is released, including consultation with the AI Deployment Committee for new algorithmic model baselines; (2) at least annually, including extensive independent penetration testing and a broader review of the effectiveness of governance, security, privacy, fairness and monitoring controls; (3) on an ad hoc basis, following an active model defect, vulnerability, operational exploit, material incident, significant performance or fairness degradation, major data or architecture change, new third-party dependency, regulatory development or material research finding.
For the plan and design stage, before developing or deploying an AI system, Malt defines in the design specifications its intended purpose, users, affected stakeholders, expected benefits, foreseeable misuse and potential risks. Systems are assessed in the risk mapping across privacy, security, fairness, transparency, accuracy, human rights, operational resilience and environmental considerations by the AI deployment committee. The review determines whether the system can proceed, requires additional safeguards or should not be deployed. 
In the collect and process data stage, Malt uses professional and marketplace information relevant to the service, such as skills and experience for matching and search. Malt evaluates data quality, completeness, and representativeness. Data is limited, cleaned, and tested, including for potential bias, before use. Users can correct, update, or request deletion of their information. Third-party models and AI services are subject to AI, privacy, security and contractual review. Data shared with external providers is governed by controls such as confidentiality, zero-retention policy, limited access. 
In the build, integrate, and interpret model stage, Malt’s matching systems use layered architectures combining lexical and semantic retrieval, ranking and business rules. Models, prompts, datasets, configurations and third-party dependencies are documented and versioned where relevant. Development and testing are separated from production environments, and access is controlled according to role and need. User-facing explanations focus on the purpose and limitations of AI-assisted search and recommendations rather than presenting the system as an autonomous decision-maker. Proposed candidates, and AI-generated briefs remain subject to human validation. Users can edit, reject or replace AI-generated recommendations and can use keyword search in the directory and type in manually their brief. 
Through the verify and validate stage, Malt verifies AI systems before and after material changes through a combination of automated testing, offline/online evaluation, human review, comparative experiments, security testing and fairness analysis. Malt also evaluates user group performance and potential disparities by including group analysis and counterfactual testing in which relevant characteristics are changed while professional skills and experience are held constant. These evaluations help identify differences in ranking position, visibility and exposure. 
Before release, at the deploy stage, Malt considers the evaluation results. Where appropriate, changes are introduced progressively and monitored against an approved baseline. Production systems maintain logging and traceability sufficient to investigate outputs, model versions, relevant inputs and human interventions, while respecting data-minimization requirements. Malt maintains human oversight for AI-assisted matching and recommendations. Fallback and rollback procedures are designed to allow Malt to isolate a faulty component, revert to a previously validated version or use a deterministic alternative when an AI component or external service is unavailable or behaving unexpectedly.
While in operation, Malt monitors AI systems across data quality, performance, fairness, security, reliability, user feedback and operational impact. Monitoring may include error rates, latency, anomalous behavior, user complaints, and external-provider failures. AI-related incidents may result in additional testing, changes to data or prompts, enhanced human review, rollback, temporary suspension, retraining or retirement of the affected system. Feedback from clients, freelancers, employees, researchers and other stakeholders contributes to continuous improvement.

Ubie does not use numeric capability thresholds, as we are not a foundation model developer. We apply decision criteria and governance processes instead.
Decision criteria. Severity is determined on two axes: imminence and severity of harm. Inputs are the use case, the users, the sensitivity of the data, the influence of outputs on clinical or health decisions, the degree of AI autonomy, whether human confirmation is in place, and whether an external foundation model is used. Because health and medical information can influence user behaviour, we treat three points as non-negotiable: our services provide general information; they do not constitute diagnosis or treatment; and they complement rather than replace human judgment.
How mitigations are graduated. Mitigations escalate with the assessed level of risk: (1) baseline - prompt and guardrail design, input and output filtering, disclaimers, terms of use; (2) elevated - mandatory medical review by physicians before release, sample evaluation of generative outputs, adversarial testing, and restriction of the intended purpose; (3) high - limitation of the scope of provision, access rights restricted so that highly confidential data is accessible only to the medical institution concerned, mandatory human confirmation with the original source always retrievable, and additional operational procedures and customer training; (4) unacceptable - postponement or non-release, or suspension of a feature already in service.
Generative AI and agentic AI. For generative AI features we assume that outputs of external foundation models may contain bias or hallucination, and we design for verification rather than trust: the original text is displayed by default with the AI-generated summary shown alongside (our "safety net structure"), sources are cited, and inputs and creation history are logged for ex post verification. Agentic AI systems that plan or act to a partial extent are under evaluation. Because an error in the medical domain can be irreversible, our governance for agentic capabilities requires an explicit boundary of autonomous action, a human decision point before any action affecting a patient or a medical record, transparency of the decision logic, and evaluation against the AISI Guide to Evaluation Perspectives on AI Safety in the Healthcare Sector before any phased introduction. Evaluation perspectives for agentic AI are being organised through our research organization Ubie Lab and the AISI Healthcare Sub-Working Group.
Governance. Risk assessment is performed by dedicated specialists independent of the development and business units in order to ensure objectivity. A two-layer structure - the Generative AI Promotion Team on the promotion side and the Risk and Compliance Committee (legal, security, public relations and other functions) on the risk side - shares information and deliberates trade-offs, and the Trust & Safety Team performs cross-product quality management. This structure is featured as an advanced case (Column 11) in the Appendix to the METI/MIC AI Guidelines for Business (Ver. 1.1).

TELUS Digital employs a comprehensive and multi-layered approach to protect privacy and prevent unauthorized disclosure of confidential or sensitive data. Here's an overview of the key strategies and measures:
Data Classification and Handling:
Information is categorized into four main classifications: Restricted, Confidential, Proprietary, and Public.
All information assets are labeled based on sensitivity as 'Low', 'Medium', and 'High Risk'.
Appropriate handling schemes are adopted for each label and classification.
Access Control:
Implements the principle of least privilege, allowing only authorized access necessary to complete assigned tasks.
Access is restricted on a field-by-field basis, ensuring employees only have access to the data they need.
Utilizes role-based access control (RBAC) for critical assets.
Employs strong authentication mechanisms, including two-factor authentication.
Data Protection Measures:
Implements encryption or functionally equivalent technology for data protection during transmission and storage.
Prevents data exfiltration and mitigates the effects of exfiltrated data.
Employs malware defenses and email/web browser protections to minimize attack surfaces.
Network Security:
Utilizes firewalls, intrusion detection software, and other boundary defense mechanisms.
Manages and controls network ports, protocols, and services to minimize vulnerabilities.
Implements secure configurations for network devices such as firewalls, routers, and switches.
Monitoring and Auditing:
Collects, manages, and analyzes audit logs to detect, understand, and recover from potential attacks.
Actively manages the lifecycle of system and application accounts.
Conducts continuous vulnerability assessments and remediation.
Privacy by Design:
Embraces Privacy by Design principles, embedding privacy-enhancing measures into all processes.
Implements data minimization and ensures data quality.
Employee Training and Awareness:
Conducts security skills assessments and provides appropriate training.
Raises awareness about privacy obligations and data protection responsibilities.
Incident Response:
Maintains an incident response infrastructure with defined roles, training, and communication protocols.
Records and manages security incidents, including breach descriptions and recovery procedures.

Specific risk identification practices for agentic AI capabilities, e.g., autonomous action-taking, tool use, multi-step planning (please specify): Microsoft has developed new threat modelling techniques for agentic AI and integrated them into its Security Development Lifecycle and Responsible AI Standard. These techniques reflect the distinctive risks created when AI systems combine models with tools, data sources, memory, and external environments to execute multi-step actions.
